findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials also deny the renderer
findings.body:
The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw id parsed from the subject, and does not include `checkReq.IdentityType`. Different identity types can share that id. Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0".

If an anonymous user is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, the entry `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is cached. A renderer check for X within the next 30s then hits that entry and is denied, even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant `*`. This breaks alert screenshots and reports. The reverse also applies: renderer denials leak to anonymous checks.

Include the identity type in the key, or the resolved internal user UID for users and service accounts.

findings.title: Ambiguous '_' separator in denial key causes collisions between different resources
findings.body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent folder with `_`. Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may themselves contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs map to the same key. For example, dashboard `abc` in folder `def_ghi` and dashboard `abc_def` in folder `ghi` both produce `..._abc_def_ghi`.

A denial on one resource then wrongly denies the other for the cache TTL.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey` in the same underlying cache, which makes the key spaces harder to reason about.

Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components, and use a distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_`.

findings.title: Denial cache is consulted before the fresh DB re-query, re-introducing stale denials
Every not-allowed Check now triggers a full permission DB query
findings.body:
Previously a cached permission map answered both allows and denials. Now any Check whose cached scopes don't grant access falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB. The denial cache is keyed per (name, folder), so it only protects repeat checks of the same resource.

A user with restricted access who triggers checks over many distinct resources pays one permission query per unseen denied resource. This happens with search results filtered item by item, or batch checks over hundreds of dashboards. Singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical calls.

This is a significant DB load amplification compared to before.

findings.title: Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache
findings.body:
The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the seeded map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no access.

Without the denial cache, the flow would still end in a deny. The cached perms don't allow access, the fallback DB query on the default fakeStore returns no permissions, and the result is `Allowed: false`. The test therefore passes regardless of whether the denial cache works.

The value should be `true` so that only the denial entry explains the deny. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial actually writes a denial entry.

findings.title: Disabling the client-side cache in-proc makes every Check deserialize full cached permission maps
findings.body:
With `NoopCache` on the in-proc client, every access check goes through the in-proc gRPC server. Each one performs several cache `Get`s, and each `Get` JSON-unmarshals its value: the denial entry, the user identifiers, and the full scope map for the action, which can contain thousands of entries for large instances.

Previously the authlib client cached per-check results. For hot paths such as batch or item checks this adds noticeable CPU and allocation overhead per request.

Meanwhile the remote/cloud client (line 162) still caches results, including denials, for 30s, so the newly-created-resource problem this PR targets remains in cloud mode.
